nameStory: The 'crane's-bill' name comes from the plant's distinctive seed pods, which look remarkably like the long, pointed beak of a crane. When the seeds are ready, these 'beaks' split open and dramatically curl upward, catapulting the seeds away from the parent plant. This species gets the 'long-stalked' part of its name because its flowers sit on unusually long, slender stems called pedicels.
description: Long-stalked Crane's-bill is a small, delicate annual plant that grows low to the ground in a spreading pattern. It's one of the daintier members of the geranium family, with deeply divided, lacy leaves that look almost feathery. The plant produces small pink or purple flowers on remarkably long, thin stalks that make them appear to dance above the foliage. It rarely grows taller than 12 inches and has a somewhat sprawling, weedy appearance.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small pink or purple flowers with 5 petals, each about 1/4 inch across, sitting on unusually long, thread-like stalks that can be 2-3 times longer than the leaves

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply cut, palm-shaped leaves divided into 5-7 narrow segments that feel soft and slightly fuzzy to the touch, giving them a delicate, lacy appearance

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Distinctive long, pointed seed pods that look like crane beaks, splitting into 5 curling sections when ripe with a satisfying spring-loaded action

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing annual that spreads in a loose, somewhat sprawling mat, with stems that feel weak and bendable rather than sturdy

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Slender, often reddish stems that are soft and easily bent, with a slightly hairy texture and joints where leaves attach

habitat: Long-stalked Crane's-bill is extremely rare in New England, typically found in disturbed soils, waste places, and along roadsides where the ground has been recently turned. It prefers sandy or gravelly soils and open, sunny locations. With only one confirmed observation in New England, it's considered either a rare native or an uncommon introduced species that hasn't established widely in our region.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate and young plants emerge with their characteristic deeply-cut leaves appearing in rosettes close to the ground.
seasonality.summer: Flowering occurs from late spring through summer, with the distinctive long-stalked pink flowers most visible during this time.
seasonality.fall: The crane's-bill seed pods mature and split open, launching seeds for next year's generation before the annual plant dies back.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground presence as this annual completes its life cycle, existing only as seeds in the soil waiting for spring warmth.

funFact: When the seed pods ripen, they create one of nature's most dramatic seed dispersal shows - the five sections of each 'crane's bill' suddenly spring apart with enough force to fling seeds up to 20 feet away, making an audible 'pop' that you can actually hear on quiet days!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small crane's-bills like Small-flowered Crane's-bill or Dove's-foot Crane's-bill, but the extremely long flower stalks are the dead giveaway - if the flower stems are much longer than the leaves themselves, you've found Long-stalked Crane's-bill.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse wild geraniums (Geranium species) with the colorful geraniums commonly grown in gardens and window boxes - those are actually Pelargoniums from South Africa. True geraniums like this one are much more subtle plants with smaller flowers and that distinctive crane's-bill seed pod that gives the whole group its name.
compareHints: Among New England's crane's-bills, Long-stalked stands out for its exceptionally long flower stalks and deeply dissected leaves. Wild Geranium has much larger flowers and less divided leaves, while Herb Robert has more triangular leaf segments and a strong smell. The long flower stalks of this species are longer relative to plant size than any of its relatives, making it distinctive when in bloom.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Wild geranium stands out from its cranesbill cousins by its substantial size, soft pink flowers, and preference for rich woodlands.
Among New England's wild geraniums, Herb Robert is the most delicate and lacy-looking, with much more finely divided leaves than the larger Wild Geranium.
Among New England's crane's-bills, bloody crane's-bill stands out for its deeply divided leaves that are cut almost to the base, creating very narrow segments.
Among New England's crane's-bills, rock crane's-bill is unique for its low, mat-forming growth and intensely fragrant leaves - most others grow more upright and have much less scented foliage.
Northern cranesbill is much smaller and more delicate than wild geranium, with tiny lavender flowers instead of large pink ones.
Thunberg's Geranium is much smaller and more delicate than our common Wild Geranium, with more finely divided leaves and smaller flowers.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Carolina crane's-bill has the smallest flowers - much tinier than the showy inch-wide blooms of wild geranium or the medium-sized flowers of Herb Robert.
Among New England's crane's-bills, meadow crane's-bill is one of the largest and most robust, forming much bigger clumps than most relatives.

Among New England's crane's-bills, dusky crane's-bill is unique for its nearly black flowers with backward-curved petals - our native wild geranium has pink flowers that face upward, while Herb Robert has small bright pink flowers.
Among New England's crane's-bills, dove's-foot stands out for its exceptionally soft, velvety leaf texture and low, mat-forming growth habit.
Among New England's crane's-bills, this is one of the tiniest and most easily overlooked.
Purple-vein geranium stands out from other New England geraniums primarily by its bright blue flowers - most other species have pink, white, or purple blooms.

Among New England's crane's-bills, cut-leaved crane's-bill stands out for having the most finely divided leaves - while wild geranium has broader, less deeply cut leaves and Herb Robert has more triangular leaf segments, cut-leaved crane's-bill looks almost feathery.
Among New England's crane's-bills, little-robin is the tiniest - much smaller than wild geranium or Herb Robert.

Richardson's geranium differs from New England's common wild geranium by having paler flowers with more prominent dark veining, perfectly straight (not curved) seed beaks, and more finely divided leaf segments.
Wood crane's-bill differs from our native wild geranium by having more deeply dissected leaves and typically stronger purple coloring with more prominent petal veining.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Siberian Crane's-bill would be one of the smallest and most delicate-looking species.
